questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Describe the fixed exchange rates adopted after the 1930s.
questions.stem: Line 1 of the clinician's note describes a patient whose blood pressure is held steady by a daily dose of medication rather than allowed to wander. Which statement best describes the fixed exchange rates the world adopted after the 1930s?

options.text: Currencies were pegged at set rates and adjusted only under agreed rules and circumstances
Currencies were left to float freely, with the central bank setting rates only when the market closed
options.misconception: describes a floating system as the postwar settlement

options.text: Currencies were tied to the gold price of the day, so the rate changed every morning
options.misconception: misreads a fixed parity as a daily float

options.text: Currencies were fixed by bilateral commercial treaties between each pair of trading countries
options.misconception: invents a system of bilateral commercial fixings

questions.explanation: Each currency was pegged at a par value and could be changed only under stated rules, which avoided both the frozen parities of the gold standard and the competitive devaluations of the 1930s.
questions.hint: Ask what the rules allowed and when.

questions.stem: Row 2 of the chart in the file shows the dollar price of gold fixed at 35 dollars an ounce in 1934, other major currencies pegged to the dollar at published rates, and the suspension of gold convertibility for exports in August 1971. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The gold price was adjusted each year to keep the dollar's purchasing power steady
options.misconception: assumes an annual adjustment of the gold price

options.text: The dollar's gold link was the anchor under the pegged system until convertibility was suspended
The other currencies were pegged to gold directly rather than to the dollar
options.misconception: reverses which currencies the others were pegged to

options.text: The suspension in 1971 shows that gold convertibility had already been withdrawn in 1934
options.misconception: misreads the 1934 price fixing as a withdrawal

questions.explanation: The dollar's gold link was the pivot for every other parity, and it was abandoned when gold outflows made the promise untenable. That is why the end of convertibility marks the end of the system.

options.text: The disagreement was mainly about how much aid each state would receive after the war
options.misconception: misdescribes the disagreement as being about aid

options.text: The British plan proposed to keep imperial trade preferences, while the American plan proposed a common external tariff
options.misconception: reduces the disagreement to a question of trade preferences

The disagreement concerned the pace of German reconstruction, which dominated the conference
options.misconception: misplaces the disagreement on German policy

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The domestic bargain behind the fixed rates
questions.learningObjective: Explain the bargain that made the fixed rate system workable.
questions.stem: Item 4 on the review sheet asks why the fixed rates held for so long when the countries involved could not always afford them. Explain the bargain that made the system workable.

answer.exemplar: The fixed rates worked because two sides made a deal with each other. Countries were expected to keep growth high and unemployment low, which their voters demanded, and they were expected to hold their parities even when that hurt their own exporters. The United States, which had the world's largest surplus, accepted that obligation because the arrangement gave the world the dollar liquidity it needed for growth and for rebuilding. None of this would have worked without controls on the movement of money, which kept speculative flows from overwhelming the pegs.

questions.explanation: The bargain let countries run full-employment policies while holding their parities, with the reserve currency absorbing the imbalance. Capital controls were what made that combination possible.
questions.hint: Ask what each side gave up to keep the pegs.

questions.topic: What the first trade agreement bound
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the first postwar trade agreement bound.

stimulus.body: Note in the chart: The patient's new drug is dosed at a fixed level and we do not adjust it week by week to suit each reading; we adjust only when the specialist reviews the case and the notes justify a change. The pharmacy still dispenses at the recorded dose whatever the patient's weight that month, so that everyone reading the chart sees the same regime.

questions.stem: Note 5 in the case folder describes a fixed dose that changes only on review. Which historical point does the note correctly support about the first trade agreement of the postwar settlement?

options.text: The agreement set no tariff levels at all and left every rate to be negotiated case by case
options.misconception: claims no rates were bound at all

options.text: The agreement required the removal of all barriers to trade in services and agriculture
options.misconception: invents coverage of services and agriculture

options.text: The agreement bound the members' internal tariffs so that a common market could follow
options.misconception: mistakes external bindings for internal free trade

options.text: The agreement bound agreed tariff rates and applied them to all members on the same terms

questions.explanation: The first trade agreement bound negotiated tariff rates and extended them to every member on the same terms, which made reciprocal cuts possible. It left internal barriers and much of agriculture untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what a bound rate means for later negotiation.

options.text: The voting rule reserves the gravest decisions for an overwhelming majority of the members
The voting rule gives an absolute veto to whichever members hold the largest quotas
options.misconception: misreads the higher threshold as a permanent veto for the largest members

options.text: The market tied the heavy industry of France and Germany together so that war became self-defeating

questions.topic: Trade creation and trade diversion
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish trade creation from trade diversion.
questions.stem: Row 8 of the chart shows two cases: a country that buys a good from a cheaper partner inside the market instead of from an expensive supplier outside it, and another that switches from the cheapest supplier in the world to a dearer partner inside the market. Which reading of the two cases is correct?

options.text: The first case is trade diversion and the second is trade creation
options.misconception: reverses the two cases

options.text: Both cases are trade creation because trade volume rose in each
options.misconception: equates trade creation with any increase in volume

options.text: The first case is trade creation and the second is trade diversion
Both cases are trade diversion because both involve buying inside the market
options.misconception: treats buying inside the market as diversion in all cases

questions.explanation: Trade creation means switching to cheaper goods inside the market. Trade diversion means switching to dearer goods inside from a cheaper supplier outside, which helps insiders and hurts outsiders.
questions.hint: Ask whether the price paid rose or fell in each case.

questions.stem: Entry 9 in the clinical record asks why the designers of the postwar currency system rejected a return to the gold standard as it had operated before the First World War. Which reason fits best?

options.text: Because the gold standard required currencies to be pegged, which the new system abandoned
options.misconception: reverses what the new system kept

options.text: Because the gold standard could not cope with the economic damage of the war
options.misconception: understates the problem as wartime damage only

options.text: Because the new system gave every country the right to change its parity whenever it wished
options.misconception: describes the new system's rules wrongly

options.text: Because the interwar gold standard had produced rigid parity, deflation and competitive devaluations

questions.explanation: The interwar experience offered two bad models, a rigid gold standard that forced deflation, and a competitive scramble of devaluations that wrecked trade. The new rules were built to steer between them.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Explain why suspending gold convertibility in 1971 mattered so much.
questions.stem: Item 10 on the review sheet explains what the world lost when the dollar stopped being convertible into gold. Explain why the suspension of convertibility in 1971 mattered more than an ordinary adjustment.

answer.exemplar: The suspension of convertibility in August 1971 was not a change in one exchange rate but the withdrawal of the promise on which the whole system rested. As long as the dollar could be exchanged for gold at a fixed price, every other parity was anchored to it, and the supply of dollars to the world was limited by the size of the American gold stock. Once the promise was withdrawn, that anchor was gone, and the rates at which currencies were quoted became market judgements rather than published rules. The Smithsonian agreement that followed tried to rebuild the pegs on a new gold price, but it did not hold, and by 1973 the major currencies were floating.

questions.explanation: The dollar's convertibility was the anchor for every other parity and the limit on the world's supply of dollars. Suspending it changed the rules of the system rather than adjusting one rate within it.
questions.hint: Ask what the anchor for the other parities was.

options.misconception: turns a negotiated outcome into a simple vote

questions.topic: The domestic bargain behind the fixed rates
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of capital controls in the fixed rate system.
questions.stem: Ticket 12 in the ward log pairs the fixed rates with the controls on the movement of money that the leading countries kept. Combining them, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The controls were introduced after the pegs had already failed and were a repair, not a condition
options.misconception: reverses the order of measures and conditions

options.text: The controls made the pegs workable by limiting the flows that would otherwise have overwhelmed them
The controls show that the pegs were never enforceable and were only ever symbolic
options.misconception: treats the pegs as symbolic

options.misconception: says the controls implied acceptance of floating

questions.explanation: A pegged rate is vulnerable to large money movements that have nothing to do with trade. Controls on those movements kept the parities credible, and their removal in the late 1970s is part of why the pegs failed.

questions.learningObjective: State the equal treatment principle and its effect.
questions.stem: Line 13 of the clinician's note records that the members agreed to extend any tariff concession they received to all other members. Which principle does that describe?

options.text: The rule that each member must apply the lowest tariff any member has negotiated to everyone
options.misconception: reverses the rule into a lowest-rate floor for outsiders

options.text: The rule that members must remove all tariffs on goods from the smallest members
options.misconception: invents a special rule for small members

The rule that members may withdraw a concession if a competitor offers a lower rate
options.misconception: invents a right to withdraw concessions

questions.explanation: The rule of equal treatment means any concession granted to one member is extended to all, so a bilateral bargain becomes multilateral. That is what keeps the number of separate negotiations manageable.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Trade creation and trade diversion
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a customs union can transfer costs to outsiders.
questions.stem: Item 16 on the review sheet asks why a common market can leave some countries worse off. Explain how a regional arrangement can transfer a cost to outsiders.

answer.exemplar: A customs union removes tariffs among its members and puts a common tariff on imports from outside. The lower prices inside the union are a real gain for its members, but the common tariff is a cost for everyone who sells into the union from outside. If a member's own producers are dearer than the best suppliers in the world, then trade inside the union shifts towards those dearer producers and away from the outside suppliers, and the outside suppliers lose the business they had before the union existed. The union has therefore created trade among its members at the expense of trade with third countries, and a state that relies heavily on exports to the union can be worse off than before.

questions.explanation: A common external tariff diverts buying from cheaper outside suppliers towards dearer suppliers inside the union. That transfer of trade is why a customs union can harm third countries even while its own members gain.
questions.hint: Ask who loses the business when the tariff changes.

stimulus.body: Note in the chart: The old ward used to set the patient's drip rate by whatever the ward sister judged to be right that morning, and the night staff would set a different rate if they were busy. When the numbers were read in the morning nobody could say what the correct rate was supposed to be. We now write the rate on the chart once, and any change has to be signed for, so that the treatment is the same whoever is on duty.

options.text: Currencies were revalued continuously by market demand, and the rules merely recorded the outcome
options.misconception: mistakes a market float for a rule-bound adjustment

options.text: Currencies were pegged at published parities, and adjustment was a deliberate, rule-bound act
Currencies were pegged only against the dollar and could never be changed against gold
options.misconception: mistakes the dollar peg for a gold peg

options.text: Currencies were free to move, but governments limited how far they could move in a year
options.misconception: describes a band around a float

questions.explanation: The note captures the defining feature of the new system: a published parity that did not drift with daily demand, and a change only through a declared process. That is what set it apart from the interwar scramble.

The fixed rates obliged every country to run a balanced budget and a surplus of exports

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the first trade agreement bound
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits built into the first trade agreement.
questions.stem: Item 21 on the review sheet asks why the first trade agreement was described as a modest step rather than a free trade area. Explain the limits that were built into it.

answer.exemplar: The agreement was modest by design and by limitation. It bound the tariff rates that the members had negotiated among themselves, and it made the equal treatment rule apply so that every concession was extended to all, which allowed cuts to be reciprocal and gradual rather than a single dismantling. But it did not remove the tariffs that members levied on each other, so the internal market remained incomplete. It did not cover services, and agriculture was only partly addressed. Several countries also entered an exception list, which meant that a portion of their trade was not covered at all. It was therefore an instrument for negotiation and gradual liberalisation rather than a customs union or a free trade area.

questions.explanation: The agreement bound external tariffs and extended concessions equally, but left internal barriers, services and much of agriculture alone. That is why it was a framework for negotiation rather than a free trade area.
questions.hint: Ask what the agreement did not cover.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two rival plans at the 1944 conference
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the fund with quotas suited the country that needed it most.
questions.stem: Item 27 on the review sheet describes the 1944 conference and the institution that emerged from it. Explain why a fund with quotas suited the country that needed it most.

answer.exemplar: The country that needed the new institution most was the one whose economy had been broken by the war and whose currency had been overvalued for decades, and it had a strong claim on the resources of the others. A fund financed by quotas gave each member a share of the decision-making that matched its share of the economy, so the largest creditor could not simply be outvoted, and it gave the largest creditor a formal interest in seeing the system work. The alternative design on the table would have distributed credit symmetrically and automatically, which suited a trading nation whose imbalances were expected to be small but suited the heavily indebted country far less well, and which the main creditor refused.

questions.explanation: Quota shares matched economic weight, which protected the main creditor's voting position while giving it a stake in the fund's success. The alternative design distributed credit by need rather than weight.
questions.hint: Ask how voting power and money were linked.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reasoning behind the postwar currency rules.
questions.stem: Item 33 on the review sheet asks why the designers of the postwar currency system did not simply restore the gold standard of the 1920s. Explain the reasoning in terms of the failures the designers wanted to avoid.

answer.exemplar: The gold standard of the 1920s and early 1930s failed in two different ways, and the designers wanted to avoid both. Where the parity was rigid, the adjustment fell on prices and wages, and countries that could not lower them faced unemployment and deflation that fed political extremism. Where governments gave up and devalued in competition, the result was a scramble of exchange controls, tariffs and collapsing trade, which made the depression far worse for everyone. A system of parities that were fixed in normal times but could be changed openly, and often, in the face of a fundamental imbalance, was designed to sit between those two failures. It required an institution to supply the finance that a change of parity could not provide on its own.

questions.explanation: The designers were avoiding rigidity on one side and competitive devaluation on the other. Adjustable parities with a lender of last resort were meant to steer between them.
questions.hint: Ask which two failures the new rules avoided.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a regional market was built
questions.learningObjective: Explain why supranational institutions were needed in the European project.
questions.stem: Item 39 on the review sheet asks why European planners put so much effort into building institutions that could settle disputes between states and firms. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The planners had watched the European states of the previous half century fail at exactly this task. Treaties had been signed and then ignored, arbitration had been refused at the moment it mattered, and economic disputes over coal and steel had been one of the causes of the two wars that had just ended. So the new arrangements were given powers and procedures of their own: a common external tariff set by the union itself, rules of competition written into the treaty and open to complaint, and a court that could give binding rulings and enforce them against member governments and against firms. The point was to take the enforcement of agreements away from the changing goodwill of national governments and place it in institutions that would still be there when those governments changed.

questions.explanation: European planners wanted enforcement that did not depend on the goodwill of national governments, because treaties had failed before. Supranational institutions and a court were meant to settle disputes without war.
questions.hint: Ask why treaties had failed to hold before 1945.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the first trade agreement bound
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the first trade agreement bound a method rather than a target.
questions.stem: Item 45 on the review sheet asks why the first trade agreement is often described as an agreement to negotiate rather than an agreement to liberalise. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The agreement is described that way because what the members actually bound was a method and a floor, not a target. They bound the tariff rates they had negotiated, so that no member could raise a rate without renegotiating, and they agreed that every concession made to one member would be extended to all the others. The actual reductions were left to successive rounds of reciprocal bargaining, with the lists drawn up at the conference and the rounds themselves to follow. There was also a grandfather clause, which allowed existing national legislation to stand even where it conflicted with the rules, and several members entered exceptions covering a share of their trade. The result was a framework that made bargaining compulsory and predictable, and made the pace of liberalisation a matter of negotiation rather than of treaty.

questions.explanation: What was bound was a floor and a method, not a complete programme of cuts. The rounds that followed did the actual liberalising, and exceptions and grandfather clauses narrowed even that.
questions.hint: Ask what was fixed in advance and what was left open.

options.misconception: confuses the peg with an indefensible defence

options.text: A published parity, adjusted under stated rules when a fundamental imbalance appears

questions.explanation: The defining feature was a published parity with a rule-bound adjustment for fundamental imbalances. That combination was the intended answer to both the rigidity of the gold standard and the devaluations of the 1930s.
questions.hint: Ask when a change was permitted.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the dollar's gold promise could not be kept.
questions.stem: Entry 50 in the clinical record asks why the dollar's gold promise could not be kept in the late 1960s. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Because the other currencies had all been revalued against gold at higher rates by then
options.misconception: invents a general revaluation of the other currencies

options.text: Because the country's spending and commitments abroad had grown beyond what its gold holdings could support
Because the gold standard had been abandoned by international agreement in 1968
options.misconception: invents a formal abandonment in 1968

options.text: Because the reserve currency's government had chosen to withdraw the metal from its vaults
options.misconception: attributes the outflow to a deliberate withdrawal of metal

questions.explanation: The dollar's liabilities abroad had grown with the world economy while the gold stock did not, so keeping the promise meant paying out gold faster than it could be justified. The outflow, not a decision, ended the promise.
questions.hint: Ask what grew faster than the gold stock.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two rival plans at the 1944 conference
questions.learningObjective: Describe the core disagreement between the two 1944 plans.

stimulus.body: Note in the chart: The two plans on the desk came from different desks. One was written by a man who spent his nights at the hotel arguing that his country's problems were financial and that a clearing house would settle them, and the other by a man who said the problem was that his country owed too much and that the money had to be found before anything else. Neither would sign the other's plan, and neither would admit the other's diagnosis of the illness.

questions.stem: Note 51 in the case folder describes two diagnoses that its author calls incompatible. Which historical point does the note correctly support about the 1944 conference?

options.text: The two delegations had already agreed on the aims and differed only on the name of the body
options.misconception: claims the aims were agreed and only the name was disputed

options.text: One delegation walked out of the conference and its plan was adopted by the remainder
options.misconception: invents a walkout and a substitution

options.text: The two plans rested on different diagnoses of the problem, and the institutional design followed the accepted one
The conference adopted a plan that mixed both diagnoses equally
options.misconception: invents an equal mixture of the two plans

questions.explanation: The note catches the real disagreement: one view saw a settlement problem, the other a debt problem. The institution written into the articles followed the accepted diagnosis, and the rival was left out.
questions.hint: Ask what the two plans each thought the problem was.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The domestic bargain behind the fixed rates
questions.learningObjective: Explain how domestic policy and the exchange rate were reconciled.
questions.stem: Item 52 on the review sheet asks how a country could hold its currency steady and still pursue a policy of high employment. Explain the mechanism that made that combination possible.

answer.exemplar: The two aims were reconciled by dividing the work between the exchange rate and the domestic economy. Inside the country, governments were left free to manage demand, since the constraint they faced was not the exchange rate but their own labour markets and prices. Outside it, they were bound to hold the parity, which ruled out the cheapest way of relieving domestic unemployment, namely devaluing to make exports cheaper. The reason they accepted that constraint was the bargain at the centre of the system: the country that issued the reserve currency supplied the world with the dollars it needed for growth and for paying for imports, and in exchange the world accepted parities that kept the United States relatively free to run its own policy. Controls on short-term capital movements made the arrangement work in practice, since the pegs could not have held against large flows of money that had nothing to do with trade.

questions.explanation: Domestic policy and the parity were separated: governments managed demand at home and held the exchange rate for external reasons. Capital controls and the reserve currency's liquidity made the division workable.
questions.hint: Ask which part of policy the peg constrained.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the first trade agreement bound
questions.learningObjective: Combine equal treatment with the reciprocal lists of reductions.
questions.stem: Ticket 53 in the ward log pairs the equal treatment rule with the round-by-round lists of tariff reductions. Combining them, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Each round had to cover every product in every member's schedule before it could count
options.misconception: requires full coverage in each round

options.text: Reciprocal lists plus equal treatment let a few negotiations liberalise a large share of trade
Equal treatment obliged members to extend concessions to outside countries as well
options.misconception: extends the rule beyond the members

options.text: The lists fixed each member's tariff for the whole period with no further negotiation
options.misconception: denies further rounds

questions.explanation: The two devices multiply each other's effect: a cut negotiated between two members was extended to all, so a few rounds covered far more trade than the number of bargains suggests. Coverage grew over time rather than at once.
questions.hint: Ask what each device did to the other.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A decision rule for a club of a hundred
questions.learningObjective: Describe the fund's decision rule in one statement.
questions.stem: Line 54 of the clinician's note describes a club in which one member holds a large share of the votes and in which the gravest decisions need a very large share of all votes. Which statement best describes the arrangement?

options.text: Voting weight follows financial contribution, and the heaviest decisions need broad agreement to pass
Every member has one vote and the heaviest decisions need a simple majority
options.misconception: describes a one-vote-per-member rule with a simple majority

options.text: The heaviest decisions are left entirely to the member with the largest share of votes
options.misconception: makes the largest member a sole decision maker

options.text: Voting weight is decided by the order in which members joined the club
options.misconception: invents a seniority rule for votes

questions.explanation: Votes were tied to quotas, so contributions and influence ran together, and the heaviest matters required a share of the total votes well beyond a simple majority. The design balances weight against breadth.
questions.hint: Ask what a member's votes are based on.

questions.learningObjective: Read the concerns behind the European project.
questions.stem: Row 55 of the chart lists the concerns behind the European project: preventing another war between the members, gaining access to a larger market, and building institutions that would make national governments less able to reverse the arrangement. Which reading does that list support?

options.text: The project was designed to create a single state with one government and one army
options.misconception: turns the project into a unitary state

options.text: The project was built mainly to raise the price of European agricultural goods
options.misconception: reduces the motive to agricultural prices

options.text: The project was intended to end American involvement in European affairs as quickly as possible
options.misconception: makes the aim a quick end to American involvement

options.text: The project sought security and growth, and used supranational authority to make the settlement durable

questions.explanation: Security and economic size were the aims, and supranational authority was the method for making the result stick, since national governments could not undo it easily. Nothing in the list points to a single state.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Trade creation and trade diversion
questions.learningObjective: Explain how members of a customs union can gain while outsiders lose.
questions.stem: Entry 56 in the clinical record asks why a country inside a customs union may gain while a country outside it loses. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: The union's members buy more from one another, so some of the trade the outsider used to win is now kept inside
The union's members pay lower tariffs, so outsiders can no longer afford to sell into it
options.misconception: claims outsiders cannot afford to sell in

options.text: The outsider's products are of lower quality than those made inside the union
options.misconception: invents a quality difference as the cause

options.text: The outsider is charged a higher rate of duty than the members pay on each other's goods
options.misconception: misstates how the common tariff works

questions.explanation: Inside the union, members buy from one another, and part of the trade that outsiders used to win is now retained within the bloc. That is why members gain and outsiders lose at the same time.
questions.hint: Ask where the outsider's old sales go.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Read the interwar experience as the problem the new rules addressed.
questions.stem: Row 57 of the chart shows the interwar experience: departures from gold in 1931 and 1933, an agreement among the main currencies in 1936, exchange controls and new tariffs in the following years, and falling trade between the partners. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The gold standard survived until the war because countries were unwilling to leave it
options.misconception: claims the gold standard survived to the war

options.text: The interwar experience showed that fixed rates worked well when trade was shrinking
options.misconception: reads the collapse as a success

options.text: Leaving gold and competing with each other produced controls, tariffs and collapsing trade
The interwar problems began only after the trade wars had already caused a fall in output
options.misconception: reverses the order of cause and effect

questions.explanation: The sequence shows how competitive departures from gold were answered with controls and tariffs, and how trade between the partners fell. That record is what the postwar rules were designed to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what the departures were answered with.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the dollar rather than gold became the working reserve.
questions.stem: Item 58 on the review sheet asks why the world came to hold reserves and settle balances mainly in the dollar rather than in gold. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Gold was awkward as the working reserve: it was heavy, it cost money to move, and the countries that had it did not want to see it leave. The dollar solved the practical problem because it was already the currency in which most international trade was invoiced and the unit in which imbalances were settled, so a government holding dollars could use them directly rather than converting first. The gold link gave the dollar a measurable anchor that anyone could check, and that measurability is what made it acceptable to hold large balances of paper claims on a country. The position was therefore self-reinforcing, and it also carried a cost for the issuer, since the world wanted the currency mainly because the issuing country was prepared to supply it and to accept the imbalance that supply created.

questions.explanation: The dollar was practical to hold and use, and the gold link gave it a checkable anchor, which made large balances acceptable. Holding it made sense because it was the currency you needed anyway.
questions.hint: Ask why dollars were easier to use than gold.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two rival plans at the 1944 conference
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the conference adopted the plan it did.

stimulus.body: Note in the chart: The plan the patient was put on was worked out by the consultant who had spent the afternoon at the library reading the old casebooks. The plan written at the other end of the hospital was better argued and more original, and it is the one that went into the notes. Nobody in the room wanted the first plan, and nobody could say quite why, but the older plan had the advantage that everyone in the room already knew what it would mean on Monday morning.

questions.stem: Note 59 in the case folder describes a conference room that adopted the familiar plan over the better argued one. Which historical point does the note correctly support about the 1944 conference?

options.text: The conference chose the plan with the strongest written argument, and the other was rejected on its merits
options.misconception: reverses which plan was adopted and why

options.text: The conference was unable to agree on any plan and handed the work to a later meeting
options.misconception: claims the conference produced nothing

options.text: The conference adopted the plan written by the delegation that supplied the chair
options.misconception: reduces the outcome to the chair's preference alone

options.text: The conference adopted the plan that most delegations were already prepared to operate

questions.explanation: The note captures the practical reason the fund with quotas was written in: it was the plan most delegations were ready to operate, while the rival would have required everyone to learn a new mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask which plan the room was prepared to use.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The domestic bargain behind the fixed rates
questions.learningObjective: Combine the fund's lending with the rules on changing a parity.
questions.stem: Ticket 60 in the ward log pairs the fund's lending with the rules permitting a currency to be changed. Combining them, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The lending existed so that the fund could choose the parities of member countries
options.misconception: invents the fund as a setter of parities

options.text: The rules for changing a currency existed so that adjustments could be made without any consultation
options.misconception: denies any role for consultation

options.text: The lending and the adjustment rules together made an open adjustment safer than a defended peg
The rules for changing a currency were designed so that adjustments would be rare and infrequent
options.misconception: contradicts the purpose of the adjustment rules

questions.explanation: The two provisions worked together: a country that could borrow the currency it needed while adjusting had less reason to defend an unsustainable peg, so an open change of parity became the safer course.
questions.hint: Ask what a country could borrow while it adjusted.
